purpose: Zolpidem is used to help you fall asleep if you have trouble sleeping, a condition called insomnia. It helps you get to sleep faster and stay asleep longer so you wake up feeling more rested. It is meant to be used short-term, usually for just a few weeks.
how_it_works: Zolpidem works by calming your brain so it can relax and let you fall asleep. It does this by boosting the effect of a natural chemical in your brain called GABA, which acts like a natural 'slow down' signal. Think of it like turning down the volume on all the busy thoughts and activity in your brain so sleep can happen naturally.
common_side_effects: Drowsiness or feeling groggy the next morning, dizziness, headache, feeling like you have a hangover, upset stomach, or feeling unsteady on your feet. Some people notice memory problems or feel a little 'foggy' the day after taking it.
warnings: Do not drive or operate heavy machinery the morning after taking zolpidem because it can still make you drowsy, especially the extended-release form. Some people have done things in their sleep like sleepwalking, sleep-driving, or eating without remembering it — tell your doctor right away if this happens. Avoid alcohol while taking this medication. It can be habit-forming, so only take it exactly as prescribed and do not take it longer than your doctor recommends. Tell your doctor if you have a history of depression, substance use, or breathing problems like sleep apnea.
typical_dosing: The usual dose for adults is 5 mg for women and either 5 mg or 10 mg for men, taken right before bedtime. You should only take it when you have at least 7 to 8 hours before you need to wake up. Never take more than prescribed, and only take it when you truly need it.
